books.title: Up from Slavery
books.author: Booker T. Washington
books.desc: Born into slavery in Virginia, Booker T. Washington tells how he fought for an education and founded the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama.
about: Washington recalls his childhood as an enslaved boy on a Virginia plantation, and the family's move after emancipation to Malden, West Virginia, where he worked in a salt furnace and a coal mine while trying to learn to read. Determined to study, he made his way to the Hampton Institute, where General Samuel Armstrong became his mentor. In 1881 Armstrong recommended him to lead a new school for Black students at Tuskegee, Alabama, which began in a run-down shanty and a church.

The autobiography presents Washington's belief in education, hard work, practical skills and self-reliance as the path to progress for African Americans. Its full text of his 1895 Atlanta Exposition Address, which called for cooperation between the races in the South, also reflects the compromise with segregation for which he was later criticised.
Up from Slavery was published in 1901 and became Washington's best-known work.
books.author_short: American educator, author and orator (1856–1915), born into slavery, founder of the Tuskegee Institute.
author_long: Booker Taliaferro Washington was born into slavery on 5 April 1856 near Hale's Ford, Virginia. After emancipation he studied at the Hampton Institute, and in 1881 became the first head of the new Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. Between 1890 and 1915 he was the most influential leader of the African-American community. He died at Tuskegee on 14 November 1915.

His autobiography Up from Slavery (1901) became a major text. After his death he was criticised for accommodating white supremacy, while defenders pointed to his long-term aim of ending the disenfranchisement of African Americans.

books.title: Antony and Cleopatra
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.desc: The Roman general Mark Antony, torn between his duty to Rome and his passion for Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt, heads towards ruin.
about: Mark Antony, one of the three rulers of the Roman world with Octavius Caesar and Lepidus, lingers in Alexandria with Cleopatra, neglecting his duties. Called back to Rome by the threat of Pompey, he makes peace with Octavius and marries his sister Octavia, but soon returns to Egypt. War breaks out between the two men. At the battle of Actium, Cleopatra's ships flee and Antony follows her, and even his loyal lieutenant Enobarbus begins to doubt him.
Shakespeare's tragedy contrasts the discipline of Rome with the splendour and pleasures of Egypt, and portrays one of his most complex heroines, whose "infinite variety" fascinates Antony to the end.

The play was probably first performed around 1607 by the King's Men. It was first printed in the First Folio of 1623, from which this English text, in its original spelling, is taken; the play draws on Thomas North's 1579 translation of Plutarch's Lives. The French translation is by François Guizot.

books.title: Uncle Silas
books.author: Sheridan Le Fanu
books.desc: After her father's death, a young heiress is sent to live with her mysterious uncle, a man long suspected of murder, in his crumbling mansion.
about: Maud Ruthyn, a young heiress, lives with her rich and reclusive father Austin Ruthyn at Knowl. Her father's brother Silas has long been under suspicion since a man to whom he owed a large gambling debt was found dead in a locked room of his house at Bartram-Haugh. Her father engages a sinister French governess, Madame de la Rougierre, who frightens Maud. On her father's death, his will places Maud in the care of Uncle Silas, whom he wishes to clear of suspicion, and she goes to live at Bartram-Haugh with his son Dudley and his daughter Milly.
Told by Maud herself, Le Fanu's novel is a classic of Victorian Gothic suspense, combining a locked-room mystery, an isolated heroine and a growing sense of menace.

Uncle Silas was first serialised in the Dublin University Magazine in 1864 under the title Maud Ruthyn and Uncle Silas, and appeared in December 1864 as a three-volume novel published by Richard Bentley in London.

books.title: The Man Who Laughs
books.author: Victor Hugo
books.desc: In late seventeenth-century England, a boy whose face was mutilated into a permanent grin grows up as a travelling performer and discovers a secret about his birth.
about: On a winter night on the English coast, a band of child-traffickers, the comprachicos, abandon a young boy. Wandering through a snowstorm, he rescues a baby girl whose mother has frozen to death. The two children are taken in by Ursus, a vagabond philosopher and mountebank, and his wolf Homo. Fifteen years later, the boy, Gwynplaine, whose mouth has been mutilated into a perpetual grin, is a famous performer, and he loves the blind Dea. Then the scheming Barkilphedro, the duchess Josiana and the court of Queen Anne enter his life.
Hugo's novel is a powerful attack on aristocratic privilege and social injustice, in which the deformed Gwynplaine becomes a symbol of the suffering people.

L'Homme qui rit was published in April 1869. A note at the end of the French text states that it was begun in Brussels on 21 July 1866 and finished there on 23 August 1868. This edition offers the French original and an anonymous English translation.

books.title: The Man Who Would Be King
books.author: Rudyard Kipling
books.desc: Two British adventurers set out from India to make themselves kings of remote Kafiristan, beyond the Afghan mountains.
about: The narrator, a newspaper editor in India, meets two penniless adventurers, Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan, who are, like him, Freemasons. They tell him that India is not big enough for them and that they intend to go to Kafiristan, a remote region of Afghanistan, armed with rifles and their military experience, to set themselves up as kings. Two years later, a broken and crippled man comes into the narrator's office at night and tells him what happened.

Kipling's story is a tale of adventure and ambition, and a parable about imperial power, pride and its fall. Its portrayal of the people of Kafiristan and of the adventurers' plans reflects the imperial outlook of its time.
"The Man Who Would Be King" was first published in 1888 in The Phantom 'Rickshaw and Other Tales.
